title: Square, Level and Setting Out
subtitle: Shapes and Measurements
framework: Professor Adow TVET — Shapes and Measurements (ADOW-SM)
_voice: Daniel. The school's voice, owner's choice 2026-09-24.

brand.name: Professor Adow TVET
brand.by: A short unit lecture from Professor Adow TVET

objectives: Explain what square, level and plumb each mean and which tool proves each.
Read a spirit level, including which way the work must move.
Prove a rectangle square by measuring both diagonals.
Set out a right angle on the ground using the 3-4-5 rule.
Calculate the number of units a measured area needs.
Add an allowance for waste and state the percentage used.

beats.say: Work that is nearly right does not stop being wrong. A frame with a lean in it will take a door that never shuts. Before anything is fixed, it is proved square, level and plumb — three different words.
Square means two things meeting at ninety degrees. Level means horizontal. Plumb means vertical. A wall can be plumb and still not square to the wall beside it.
Each has its own tool. The try square for the corner, the spirit level for horizontal, the plumb bob for vertical. They do not swap, and a level held upright proves nothing about a corner.
Set the level on the work and look at the vial. Here the bubble is not centred. It has run to one end, and that end is the HIGH end — a bubble is lighter than the liquid, so it floats uphill.
So the reading tells you what to do. Lower the end the bubble ran to, or pack up the other one, and it comes down to the middle. Read it, then move the work the way it told you.
A frame can have four correct sides and still be a parallelogram. The check is the diagonals: measure from this corner to the far one, then the other pair the same way.
If the two are equal, the frame is square. If they differ, push the long diagonal shorter until they are equal, and only then is it square. Two numbers settle it, and no squinting is needed.

scenes.heading: A right angle on the ground

beats.say: On the ground there is no square big enough, so the sides do the work. Measure three along one line, four along the other, and when the distance between those points is exactly five, the corner is a right angle.
Any multiple of those numbers does the same job, and bigger is better over a long building: three hundred, four hundred, five hundred, or one point five, two, two point five.
Once it is set out you can count what goes in it. Divide the length by the width of one board: four point two divided by nought point six is seven a row, and three rows makes twenty one.
Twenty one is what the job needs measured, and it is not what you order. Every cut leaves an offcut, and some of it is unusable, so an allowance for waste goes on top — ten per cent here.

Twenty one and ten per cent is twenty three point one, so you order twenty four. Always round up, because you cannot buy a tenth of a board, and say which percentage you used so the next person can check it.

So: for square, both diagonals equal. For level and plumb, the bubble, and remember which end is high. For setting out, three, four, five, then count what fits and add the waste. Prove it, then build to it.

at.prove: Prove it, then build to it
